title: Spam Email Classifier Report
text: This report investigates whether an email can be accurately classified as spam or non-spam using pre-extracted word frequencies, special character frequencies, and capitalization patterns. Using the UCI Spambase dataset of 4,601 emails, we trained a logistic regression classifier and found that the model’s test accuracy was 92.7% (F1 score of 0.906). Dollar signs, large strings of capitalized characters, and words like “free” and “remove” emerged as the strongest predictors of spam. Automated spam detection is critical because unsolicited email drains productivity and drives phishing and fraud, while overly aggressive filters risk blocking important legitimate messages. The main limitations are that the data was collected in 1999—meaning modern spam tactics have evolved—and that the non-spam emails come primarily from a single corporate environment (Hewlett-Packard Labs), limiting generalizability to broader, contemporary inboxes.

title: Spam Email Classifier Report
text:
Introduction
Email is a foundational tool for personal and professional communication, but its low cost makes it a constant target for unsolicited bulk messaging, or spam. Automated spam filters use statistical models to separate legitimate emails (“ham”) from unwanted promotional or fraudulent messages before they reach a user’s inbox. Instead of reading raw text directly, simple filters rely on numerical features—such as how frequently certain words, symbols, or capital letters appear—to predict whether a message is spam.
Solving this problem well is both practically important and technically interesting. At scale, spam wastes time, clogs server infrastructure, and serves as a primary vehicle for phishing and financial scams. At the same time, spam filtering requires balancing two asymmetric errors: letting spam into an inbox (a false negative) is an annoyance or security risk, whereas mistakenly blocking an important work or personal email (a false positive) can cause missed deadlines or lost opportunities. Identifying which simple textual patterns reliably separate spam from legitimate mail is therefore essential for building dependable email systems.
To explore this, we ask: Can we accurately classify an email as spam or non-spam using its word frequencies, special character frequencies, and capitalization patterns?
We answer this question using the Spambase dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (Hopkins et al., 1999), originally compiled at Hewlett-Packard Labs in 1999 from postmaster spam reports and filed work and personal emails. Each row represents a single email (4,601 rows total: 39.4% spam, 60.6% non-spam). Because the dataset is already preprocessed into numerical features, we use all 57 continuous predictors directly:

Word frequencies (48 variables): Percentage of words matching specific terms (e.g., free, money, remove, hp).
Character frequencies (6 variables): Percentage of characters matching ;, (, [, !, $, and #.
Capitalization patterns (3 variables): Average length, longest length, and total count of uninterrupted capital-letter sequences.

The target (response) variable is spam, a binary indicator denoting whether an email is unsolicited commercial email (1 = spam, 0 = non-spam). Because every email pairs these 57 lexical features with a labeled binary outcome, this dataset directly supports our classification question.

title: Spam Email Classifier Report
text:
Model Training and Evaluation
We split the dataset into an 80% stratified training set and a 20% stratified test set. Because the 57 predictors span different scales—percentages versus capitalization run lengths — we standardize the features inside a scikit-learn pipeline paired with logistic regression (Pedregosa et al., 2011). We use logistic regression because this is a binary classification problem and its coefficients are interpretable. The metrics we use are accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC AUC. The classes are imbalanced (39% spam) so accuracy alone is not reliable. Precision is highly useful because, in a real world sense, flagging non-spam emails as spam could have consequences. F1 balances precision and recall so it is useful for a holistic evaluation of the model.

title: Spam Email Classifier Report
text:
Results
On the held-out test set, the standardized logistic regression model separates spam (1) from non-spam (0) across varying probability thresholds. The confusion matrix details true positives and true negatives alongside false positives (legitimate emails mistakenly flagged as spam) and false negatives (spam messages reaching the inbox), illustrating the trade-off between blocking important messages and allowing unwanted or risky mail through. Complementing this fixed-threshold view, the ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate across all cutoffs relative to the diagonal chance baseline (AUC = 0.50), capturing how well the 57 lexical and capitalization features rank spam above non-spam emails overall.

title: Spam Email Classifier Report
text:
Limitations

1999 temporal snapshot: Modern spam frequently relies on URLs, image-only messages, spoofing, and evolving vocabulary rather than late-1990s bulk-email keywords.
Corporate source bias: Non-spam examples come heavily from Hewlett-Packard Labs inboxes, meaning corpus-specific terms (hp, george) reflect that specific environment rather than general user mail.
Decision threshold trade-off: Lowering the probability threshold from 0.50 increases recall (catching more spam) at the cost of higher false positives (flagging legitimate messages), whereas raising it protects legitimate mail at the expense of letting more spam through.

title: Spam Email Classifier Report
text:
Discussion
The model performed well on the test set with a 92.7% accuracy. Precision was 0.925, recall was 0.887, and its F1 score was 0.906 (Table 3). The model’s validation score (measured by the mean accuracy across 5 cross validation folds) is 91.9% (Table 2) - this is very similar to the test accuracy. This suggests that the model is not overfitting and generalizes well to unseen data. Ultimately, our question was: can we accurately classify an email as spam or non-spam using its word frequencies, special character frequencies, and capitalization patterns? Our results suggest that the answer to our question is yes.
As per Figure 2, our model flagged 26 out of 558 legitimate emails wrongly as spam whilst 41 of 363 spam emails went unflagged. These numbers suggest that 4.7% of non-spam emails will not be in the recipient’s inbox and the recipient will see 11.3% of spam emails in their inbox. False positives occur less than false negatives (26 vs 41). This is relevant because, in the real world, it is more important for non-spam, potentially priority emails to be seen by the recipient than not seeing spam emails. Our test error of 7.3% matches closely with the UCI dataset page’s stated error of approximately 7% (Hopkins et al., 1999), which is what we expected going into this. One interesting note from our results is that the strongest non-spam predictors were the words “george”, “hp”, and “meeting” (Table 5) - these words come from Hewlett-Packard Labs inboxes so they are unique non-spam indicators for these data points rather than useful general features.

Limitations

1999 temporal snapshot: Modern spam frequently relies on URLs, image-only messages, spoofing, and evolving vocabulary rather than late-1990s bulk-email keywords.
Corporate source bias: Non-spam examples come heavily from Hewlett-Packard Labs inboxes, meaning corpus-specific terms (hp, george) reflect that specific environment rather than general user mail.
Decision threshold trade-off: Lowering the probability threshold from 0.50 increases recall (catching more spam) at the cost of higher false positives (flagging legitimate messages), whereas raising it protects legitimate mail at the expense of letting more spam through.



Impact
Spam has a meaningful impact on recipients. It was estimated that spam emails cost American firms and consumers nearly 20 billion USD a year (Rao & Reiley, 2012). Using simple features, our model was able to flag 88.7% of spam emails (0.887 recall). This shows that even a basic model that uses single word/character features could be very useful in reducing human interaction with spam and, thus, the cost associated with it.


Future Iterations
It would be useful to remove the Hewlett-Packard Labs specific words such as “george” and “hp” to see whether the model still performs on more generic, less “biased” data. Additionally, adjusting the 0.5 probability cutoff may reduce the false positives so that would be a good avenue to investigate. Other models and newer data would be a natural next step. Models such as Naive Bayes or random forests (Dada et al., 2019) may perform better on more recent email data.
